## Module reference (from gemini)

### Doublet (plants): Production and injection limbs, with the children's values derived from a design.
- dispatch: string least_cost (Rule that orders the sources of a schedule)
- outages: string lowest_demand (Rule that picks the steps of the outage)
- backup: string peak|none (Redundancy sizing keeps: the boilers cover the peak or nothing)
- depth*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (True vertical depth of the reservoir midpoint)
- gradient*: number {value, unit} temperature_gradient in C/km|C/m|K/km|K/m|degC/km|degC/m|°C/km|°C/m (Increase of undisturbed rock temperature with depth)
- surface_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Ground temperature at the surface)
- permeability*: number {value, unit} permeability in m2|mD >= 0 (Permeability of the reservoir rock)
- thickness*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Gross thickness of the reservoir)
- well_diameter*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Inner diameter of both vertical wells)
- drainage_radius*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Radius of the drainage area around each well)
- roughness*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Absolute roughness of the inner wall of both vertical wells)
- nominal_flow*: number {value, unit} volume_flow in l/s|m3/h|m3/s >= 0 (Production flow the doublet and its pump are designed for)
- pump_efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Overall efficiency of the production pump)
- nominal_wellhead_pressure*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Wellhead pressure the doublet is designed for)
- ports: in return_in (brine), in power_in (electricity), out supply_out (brine)

### ProductionReservoir (subsurface): Aquifer supplying a production-well sandface stream.
- role: string production|injection (Whether the reservoir supplies production or receives injection)
- pressure*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Static reservoir pressure)
- temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Undisturbed reservoir temperature)
- permeability*: number {value, unit} permeability in m2|mD >= 0 (Permeability of the aquifer rock)
- aquifer_thickness*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Thickness of the aquifer)
- drainage_radius*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Radius of the drainage area around the well)
- top_depth*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Depth of the top of the aquifer)

## What the limits mean for the design

- One doublet at the caps (300 m3/h, 40 K, 1030 kg/m3, c_p about 4.2 kJ/kg/K) gives about 14.4 MW;
  the 30 MW heating peak needs two or three doublets, or fewer with a heat pump and a boiler.
- At 2500 m the reservoir is 87 degC, below the 100 degC supply: the heat pump share of the peak
  (ideal exchanger) is (100 - 87) / (100 - 60) = 0.325, about 9.75 MW; direct supply needs about
  3000 m or more (102 degC less the approach).
- The 20 degC cold supply favours a compression chiller (gemini's sample study ranked heat pump +
  boiler + compression chiller first; absorption needs drive water above 80 degC).
- Gas per doublet at 300 m3/h: 240 Nm3/h (192 Nm3/h CH4, about 1.9 MW of fuel): burn it in the peak
  boiler first through a `GasMakeup`, flare only the surplus.

{'name': 'knowledge/handbook-design.md', 'section': {'number': '3', 'title': '3 The subsurface', 'start': 41585, 'size': 6863}, 'start': 0, 'total': 6863, 'text': "# 3 The subsurface

This chapter gives the reservoir values a design needs and how they follow from depth: temperature,
pressure, productivity, drawdown, thermal breakthrough. Most of them are properties of the site
(the case) and only the depth and well design are choices.

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

T(z) = T_surface + G · z

with T_surface the mean surface (or reference) temperature and G the geothermal gradient. Typical
continental gradients are of the order of 25 to 35 K/km; sedimentary basins with thick insulating
cover can be higher [textbook: Stober and Bucher 2013]. The gradient of a site comes from the case
(measured wells, maps), never from a typical value.

In gemini the plant states only the depth; the case holds `site.ground.gradient` and
`site.ground.surface_temperature`, and the run derives the reservoir temperature at the plant's
depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `gemini/plants/doublet.py`].

The produced (wellhead) temperature is a little lower than the reservoir temperature because the
brine loses heat on the way up; the loss is larger at low flow and in thin wells. gemini computes
it with the wells' heat transfer coefficient (`heat_transfer_coefficient`, 0.7).

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.3 Productivity and injectivity

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

with k the permeability, h the net thickness, μ the brine viscosity, r_e the drainage radius, r_w
the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.
Notes:

- **k·h (transmissivity) is the key reservoir number.** Doubling it halves the drawdown at a given
  flow. Permeability is the most uncertain of the inputs (3.7).
- **Viscosity falls with temperature**, so the injector, taking cold brine, has a lower II than the
  producer's PI at the same k·h. Design the injection pressure for the coldest injection
  temperature.
- **Skin** captures near-well damage (positive) or stimulation (negative); a new well is often
  assumed at zero skin, which is optimistic for an injector that clogs with fines over time.
- **r_e** enters only through a logarithm; the result is not sensitive to it.

gemini derives the PI and II of a `Doublet` from the case's permeability and thickness, the brine
viscosity, the plant's `drainage_radius`, `well_diameter` and `skin` [gemini: `gemini/plants/doublet.py`].

## 3.4 Drawdown and the capacity of a doublet

A **doublet** is one production well and one injection well into the same aquifer. Its thermal
capacity is

P = ṁ · c_p · ΔT_brine = ρ Q c_p (T_prod − T_inj)

limited by:

- the **flow** the pump and the reservoir allow (3.3, 4.3), and any flow cap of the case;
- the **brine cooling** ΔT_brine, limited by the return temperature of the network plus the
  exchanger approach (6.1), by a heat pump's minimum source outlet temperature (6.4), by scaling
  limits on the cold side (5.3), or by a cap of the case;
- the **pump power**: drawdown grows linearly with flow and friction with its square, so the last
  m3/h is the most expensive.

The drawdown at flow Q is Q / PI. Keep the dynamic level (the pressure at the pump) comfortably
above the pump's minimum intake pressure (4.3, 4.4).

## 3.5 Thermal breakthrough and doublet spacing

The injected cold brine forms a cooled region that grows toward the producer. After the
**breakthrough time** the produced temperature declines. For a doublet in a homogeneous confined
aquifer [paper: Gringarten and Sauty 1975]:

V_B = π L² H (ρc)_a / ( 3 (ρc)_w ),  t_B = V_B / Q

with L the well spacing at reservoir depth, H the aquifer thickness, (ρc)_a the volumetric heat
capacity of the saturated aquifer and (ρc)_w that of water. Lessons:

- breakthrough time grows with the **square of the spacing** and linearly with thickness, and falls
  with flow;
- a spacing that delays breakthrough beyond the economic lifetime of the plant is the target;
  Dutch practice places doublets with roughly 1 to 2 km between the well bottoms [paper: Willems
  2016];
- several doublets in one reservoir interfere: give each its own drainage area.

gemini models breakthrough with the `ThermalDecline` module [gemini: `gemini/modules/subsurface/
thermaldecline.py`]. A one-year simulation cannot show decline that sets in after decades: check
t_B with a calculation and state it.

## 3.6 Choosing the depth

Depth is a design choice whenever the case allows it. Deeper wells give:

- **hotter brine** (3.1): more heat per m3, a smaller temperature lift for a heat pump, possibly a
  direct supply without a heat pump;
- **higher drilling cost**: cost per metre rises with depth; the price is the case's
  (`economics.capex.drilling`, sourced in `knowledge/data-economics.csv`), never a figure of this
  handbook;
- **a deeper pump setting and more friction**, and, with dissolved gas, more gas at a given intake
  pressure if the setting does not follow (4.4).

Search depth together with the doublet count and the heat pump capacity (Chapter 10); the optimum
depends on the price of electricity against the price of drilling.

## 3.7 Subsurface uncertainty

Before drilling, permeability and the gradient are uncertain; permeability often by a factor of
two or more. A robust design:

- is checked at the pessimistic end of each range (low k·h, low gradient) and still meets the
  demand, with a backup that covers what the geothermal side may lack (8.4);
- is reported with the range of its cost (10.5);
- names the values that matter most (a sensitivity study, 10.5), so that a test of the first well
  can confirm them.

The gradient often moves the levelised cost more than any price, because it sets the brine
temperature, the heat pump lift and the number of doublets together; permeability within its usual
range often moves it much less, as long as the pump keeps its intake margin. Check this order with
a sensitivity study on the case (10.5), never assume it.

{'name': 'knowledge/handbook-design.md', 'section': {'number': '5', 'title': '5 Brine chemistry and associated gas', 'start': 57223, 'size': 7649}, 'start': 0, 'total': 7649, 'text': "# 5 Brine chemistry and associated gas

This chapter covers what the brine carries besides heat: dissolved gas, salts, solids. Each can
stop a plant (scaling, gas-locked pumps, clogged injectors) or add emissions (methane, CO2).

## 5.1 Dissolved gas and why it comes out

Deep brines often carry dissolved gas, mainly CO2 and CH4 (and sometimes N2, H2S). The case
states it as a **gas-liquid ratio** (GLR, Nm3 of gas per m3 of liquid at standard conditions) and a
composition. A normal cubic metre is at 0 °C and 1.01325 bar(a) [standard: DIN 1343].

Gas stays dissolved while the pressure is above the bubble point. On the way up the pressure falls
and gas comes out: first in the well above the pump (two-phase flow, 4.2), then at the pump intake
if the intake pressure is low (4.4), then in surface equipment where the pressure is lowest.
Released CO2 raises the pH of the brine and drives carbonate scaling (5.3).

Two operating philosophies:

- **Keep it in solution**: hold the surface loop above the bubble point (pressurised loop),
  inject the gas back with the brine. Simpler, no gas to handle, but needs pressure margin
  everywhere, and the gas never earns anything.
- **Separate it**: degas at a controlled pressure (5.2), then use or dispose of the gas (5.5). Needed
  when the gas content is high or the gas has value as fuel; it produces emissions that must be
  counted (5.6).

## 5.2 Degassers and separators

A degasser (gas separator) lets the free gas leave the liquid in a vessel at a set pressure. Its
design values are the vessel pressure (or pressure drop) and the separation efficiency. In gemini
the `Degasser` removes a share `separation_efficiency` of the free gas and applies a pressure loss;
dissolved gas that does not come out at the vessel pressure stays in the liquid (Henry's law and
residence time are not modelled) [gemini: `gemini/modules/treatment/degasser.py`].

Place the degasser upstream of the heat exchanger so that the exchanger sees liquid only, and after
the production wells are joined, so that one vessel serves all doublets. A lower vessel pressure
releases more gas but makes scaling more likely; a design without PVT data cannot predict the
dissolved share and must say so.

For high-enthalpy fluids a **flash separator** splits steam from brine; it is used in power plants
and is not part of a low-temperature heating plant [textbook: DiPippo 2016]. gemini's
`Separator` (under `power`) is such a flash separator.

## 5.3 Scaling, corrosion and inhibitors

- **Carbonate scaling** (calcite) follows CO2 degassing and heating; it is worst where pressure
  falls and temperature is high (pump outlet, degasser, hot side of the exchanger).
- **Silica and sulphide scaling** follow cooling; they are worst on the cold side: the exchanger
  outlet and the injector. A low injection temperature raises heat output and raises this risk. If
  the chemistry is known, a minimum injection temperature may be a real design limit; take it from
  a geochemical study, never from a typical value.
- **Corrosion** follows CO2, H2S, oxygen ingress and chlorides; it governs material choice
  (titanium or stainless plates in exchangers, coated or alloy casing) and needs a closed, oxygen-free
  loop.

Scale and corrosion **inhibitors** are dosed continuously in proportion to the flow. Typical
geothermal scale-inhibitor doses are a few to some tens of ppm of product [paper: Gallup 2009, as
cited in gemini `gemini/modules/treatment/inhibitordosing.py`]. In gemini the `InhibitorDosing`
module computes the product mass flow from a dose; the chemical is priced through the case's
`opex.variable.chemical` and drawn from a `ChemicalGrid`.

Fouling of the exchanger lowers its UA over time; design for the fouled state and monitor it (gemini
reports a fouling diagnostic against `fouling_threshold` [gemini: `heatexchanger.py`]).

## 5.4 Sand and filters

Weakly consolidated sandstones produce fines and sand, which erode pumps and clog injectors.
Remedies, from the well outward: sand control in the completion, a **desander** (hydrocyclone) at
the surface, and **filters** before the exchanger and before the injector. A hydrocyclone's
pressure loss is of the order of 1 bar at design flow and its efficiency depends on particle size
against its cut size [textbook: Svarovsky 2000, as cited in gemini
`gemini/modules/treatment/desander.py`]; both are design-specific values to source from the
vendor. The sand load comes from the case (`site.fluid.sand_concentration`); the removed sand is
waste with a disposal price.

gemini models `Desander`, `Filter` (with a clogging pressure drop) and `WasteGrid` for the removed
solids.

## 5.5 What to do with the gas: flare, boiler, CHP

Once separated, the gas must go somewhere. The options, in rising order of value:

| Option | What it does | Gains | Costs and emissions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vent | releases the gas | none | methane released whole: the worst option; normally not allowed |
| Flare | burns the gas | nothing but safety | CO2 from combustion plus the CO2 in the gas; the unburnt share of methane escapes (about 2 % at 98 % combustion efficiency [standard: US EPA AP-42 13.5]) |
| Boiler | burns it for heat | heat that replaces grid gas | same CO2 as a flare, but replaces bought fuel |
| CHP (gas engine) | burns it for power and heat | electricity and heat | engine cost; electricity replaces grid power |
| Reinjection | keeps it in the brine | no emissions | needs pressure everywhere (5.1) |

Rules:

- **Burn before you flare.** If a boiler or CHP needs heat anyway, the co-produced gas is free fuel.
  Size the boiler's base fuel use to the gas available, top up with grid gas, and send only the
  surplus to the flare. In gemini a `GasMakeup` offers the co-produced gas to the burner first,
  draws the shortfall from the `GasGrid` and sends the surplus to its `excess_out`, usually a
  `Flare` [gemini: `gemini/modules/piping/gasmakeup.py`; the `Boiler` and `CHP` burn the
  co-produced gas first, `boiler.py`, `chp.py`].
- **Know the fuel value.** The heating value of the co-produced gas depends on its methane share.
  For pure methane the lower heating value is about 50.0 MJ/kg, about 35.8 MJ/Nm3 [textbook: standard
  combustion tables; the per-Nm3 figure is derived with a methane density of 0.717 kg/Nm3]. CO2 in
  the gas adds no fuel value.
- **A CHP must be able to sell or use its power**, and needs enough running hours; with little
  gas the engine is small and its specific cost high (6.6).

## 5.6 Emissions: CO2, methane and electricity

Count three sources over the period:

1. **Combustion and carried CO2**: every kg of CH4 burned forms 44/16 = 2.75 kg CO2 [derived from
   stoichiometry], plus the CO2 already in the gas, whether it is burned, flared or vented.
2. **Methane released**: vented, unburnt in a flare, or slipped in an engine, counted with its
   global warming potential. IPCC AR6 gives GWP100 = 29.8 for fossil methane [paper: Forster et al.
   2021, table 7.15]. A small methane slip
   weighs much: 2 % unburnt methane at GWP 29.8 adds about 0.6 kg CO2e per kg of methane flared,
   about a fifth of the 2.75 kg from combustion [derived].
3. **Bought electricity** times the grid's CO2 intensity. The intensity is a case value (country,
   year, average or marginal); never a typical value.

gemini's `co2` metric counts all three: direct, methane and electricity [gemini:
`gemini/study/metrics.py`]. The case's CO2 price applies only to the plant's own CO2 and methane
(CO2e), not again to grid electricity, whose price already carries its CO2 [gemini 0.6.16,
`docs/CHANGELOG.md`, QA-128].

## 6.2 Cascading: using the brine more than once

A cascade passes the brine through several users in order of falling temperature: the hottest
service first, then lower-temperature services on the cooler brine. The Lindal diagram classifies
direct uses by the temperature they need [textbook: Lindal 1973, reproduced in Stober and Bucher
2013]. In a heating and cooling plant common cascades are:

- **Exchanger, then heat pump on the brine**: the exchanger takes the heat the brine gives directly;
  the heat pump then cools the brine further (its evaporator on the brine) and lifts that heat to the
  supply temperature. This raises the heat per m3 and keeps the brine cooling within its limit.
- **Absorption chiller drive, then heating**: the hottest water drives the chiller (it needs a high
  drive temperature, 7.2) and its outlet still heats a lower-temperature service.
- **Series of exchangers on the network**: the coolest return water meets the coolest brine first.

Order users so each takes the brine at the temperature it needs and no higher.", 'score': 57, 'citation': {'document': 'handbook-design.md', 'title': 'handbook-design.md', 'page': None}, 'section': '6 Surface heat > 6.1 Heat exchangers: approach, UA and effectiveness'}, {'scope': 'knowledge', 'name': 'knowledge/handbook-design.md', 'text': "The produced (wellhead) temperature is a little lower than the reservoir temperature because the
brine loses heat on the way up; the loss is larger at low flow and in thin wells. gemini computes
it with the wells' heat transfer coefficient (`heat_transfer_coefficient`, 0.7).

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

with k the permeability, h the net thickness, μ the brine viscosity, r_e the drainage radius, r_w
the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.

messages.content:
## Role

You are an energy systems engineer of a geothermal design team, one of up to 8 engineers
working at once. You own the surface energy system: heat pumps, chillers, boilers, storage, heat
exchangers, surface pipes and the network. The design lead gives you one module group (for
example "heating" or "cooling"); you propose the values that make it meet its services, with
their sources. You propose; the design lead decides and writes the plant. You read no project
file and write no plant.

## Inputs

- The design lead's brief: your module group, the plant paths you own with gemini's issue text,
  the plant text of your modules, the case values you need with their units (services, supply
  temperatures, prices, limits; the peak, the energy and the overlap of each demand profile), the
  interface values the lead settled and the handbook chapters to read. What the brief does not
  hold, you do not have: name it in `note`.
- The module reference below: your modules, their parameters and units.

## Tools

- `describe_module`: a module that is not in the module reference below.
- `search_knowledge`: search the global Knowledge base (handbooks, cited data).
- `read_knowledge`: read one Knowledge document or one of its sections, such as a handbook
  chapter the brief names.
- `finish`: hand your proposal to the design lead.

## Rules

Workflow (few calls, short answers):

- Read the brief once. Read a handbook chapter it names once, and `describe_module` only for a
  module the reference below lacks: what a tool returned stays above in the conversation.
- Decide every value of your group, then finish once with all of them: one `changes` entry per
  plant path, `path` as the plant writes it (`params.heat_pump.nominal_capacity`) and `value` in
  the plant file's form, each with its `source` (the case path, the brief's file and page, the
  Knowledge document and section) or `assumption` with a `reason`.
- Propose only paths of your group. A path of another group, or a value that couples to the
  subsurface (the source temperature, the brine return), goes in `couplings` with your value and
  reason.
- A number only gemini gives (a heat pump's or chiller's COP and capacity at its design point,
  an exchanger's outlet) goes in `evaluations`: `module`, the operating point with its values,
  and what it decides. The lead evaluates it; never guess it.

Do and don't (from earlier runs):

- Don't put a case value into the plant: gemini answers `invalid_value ... give it in the case`.
- Don't convert a value to show it (`320.15 K (47 degC)`): copy each value with the unit the
  plant file or the case writes it in.
- Do keep a value the plant text gives when the case calls for no other: no change for it, and
  say "kept" in `note`.
- Size each machine for the share of its service it covers, from the profile's peak, energy and
  overlap in the brief, and say in its `reason` what covers the rest.
- A heat pump or a chiller works between the temperatures the case and the source give; ask its
  design point in `evaluations` when you change its capacity or temperatures.
- A network return temperature is a design choice of the team within the case's limits: when
  the case lacks it, or another one suits the plant better, propose it with its reason (the
  source, the brine cooling limit, the demand met) and name it in `couplings`.
- An equipment value no file gives (an efficiency, a fraction) is an `assumption` with a reason.
- The case's economics may price a kind by another size: a heat exchanger per W of nominal duty,
  a thermal or ice storage per MWh stored (an ice storage per cubic metre by its `volume`), a pipe
  per MW and metre. gemini then asks for the module's `nominal_duty`, `energy_capacity`, `volume`
  or a pipe's `nominal_capacity`: ask it in `evaluations` or leave it to gemini's sizing, never
  by hand.
- A value gemini asks for at a case path (`site`, `demand`, `utilities`, `time`, `economics`,
  `requirements`) belongs to the case: `case_changes` `<path>: <why>`; never put it into the
  plant under another path, and never with a number of your own.
- Compute nothing by hand: no formula, no unit conversion and no derived value in a change.
- In a superstructure, fill the parameters of every option you own, whether it may be off or
  not: the search turns options on and off.
- A value from the Knowledge keeps its source.

## Output

Finish with `finish(answer)` holding the proposal: `changes` ({path, value, source, reason}),
`evaluations` ({module, point, why}), `case_changes`, `couplings` and a `note` of at most five
lines (each machine's share of each service, your assumptions, what you kept).

## Examples

Brief "heating", issues on the heat pump, the peak boiler and the exchanger: changes for the
heat pump's capacity (the base of the heating profile), the boiler's capacity (the peak above
it) and the exchanger's approach, the Carnot fraction an assumption (no datasheet); one
evaluation of the heat pump at its design point; one coupling: the brine return temperature
(reservoir).

## Rules for every agent

- Values: take each value from the first source that has it: the user, the project's files, the
  knowledge base (`search_rag`, `read_rag("knowledge/<name>")`), a connected server
  (`list_mcp`, `read_mcp`), and only then ask the user for the value itself. Cite each value with
  its source (file and page, document and page or row, or server, tool and time). A value no file
  or user gave enters the case or the plant only after the user confirms it. Never a typical
  value, a rule of thumb or a number you recall.
- Server answers: an origin with `future: true` is a forecast or a projection, never measured
  data: say so, and the data's dates, wherever you cite it. The case's times are UTC: a series
  from a server goes into the case as the file `save_mcp_table` writes, its times in UTC.
- The user's words: say "the user said" or "the user's instruction" only for what the user wrote
  in this chat. A rule of geomind or gemini (dates without an offset are read as UTC), a file, the
  knowledge base or your own choice is named as what it is, never as the user's; a choice of yours
  is an assumption to confirm.
- Approved is settled: an answer that approves an item of your question ("approve A and B", "yes
  to 2") confirms it. Record it at once (`confirmed: true`, with the user's answer as its
  source) and never ask about it again in this chat; a follow-up question asks only what is new
  (a value gemini derived from the answer, a value the answer left open).
- No defaults: a value nothing gives stays unset and is named as missing; never fill it in.
- Units and physics: gemini converts every unit and computes every physical value. Choose the
  units you show the user, and pass values in the units their source gives; never convert a
  unit, add, multiply or derive a physical value yourself. Copy each number digit for digit.
- Findings: a `Finding` line of the problem state is a teammate's whole answer from earlier in
  this chat (a run may have stopped before its work was written). Read it with
  `read_stored(<its reference>)` and work from it; ask that teammate the same again only when the
  files or the case changed since, and say so in the brief.
- Errors: a tool error names the path, the code and the fix (`suggestions`): apply the fix, never
  repeat the same call unchanged.

## Plant file keys

The keys of a plant file, from gemini's schema; `read_plant(plant_class=...)` gives a class's whole file and `describe_module` a module's parameters (* has no default), units and ports:
format*: 1
kind*: "plant"
name*: string
about: object
type: ATESPlant|BoilerChpPlant|CoolingSubstation|DistrictEnergyPlant|DistrictNetwork|Doublet|DoubletHeatPlant|HeatingAbsorptionCoolingPlant|HeatingCoolingPlant|HeatingFullCoolingPlant|HeatingHeatPumpCoolingPlant|HeatingPlant|HeatingSubstation|MultiWellPlant|NodalDoublet|ParallelExchangerPlant
size: {name: object}
modules: {name: object}
connections[]:
  source*: string
  target*: string
  type: state|None
inlets: {name: string or object}
outlets: {name: string or object}
outputs: {name: object}
constraints[]:
  target*: string
  equals: string
  at_least: string
  by*: string
  bounds*: string or object
params: object
fluids: {name: object}
boundary: {name: object}
optional[]: string

## Module reference (from gemini)

### HeatExchanger (exchangers): Two-stream heat exchanger with thermal and fouling diagnostics.
- thermal_conductance*: number {value, unit} thermal_conductance in GW/K|MW/K|W/K|W/degC|W/°C|kW/K >= 0 (Heat transfer conductance (UA) of the exchanger)
- arrangement: string counterflow|parallel (Flow arrangement of the two streams)
- hot_nominal_pressure_drop*: number {value, unit} pressure_difference in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Pressure drop of the hot side at its nominal mass flow)
- cold_nominal_pressure_drop*: number {value, unit} pressure_difference in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Pressure drop of the cold side at its nominal mass flow)
- hot_nominal_mass_flow*: number {value, unit} mass_flow in kg/s|t/h >= 0 (Mass flow of the hot side at which its nominal pressure drop holds)
- cold_nominal_mass_flow*: number {value, unit} mass_flow in kg/s|t/h >= 0 (Mass flow of the cold side at which its nominal pressure drop holds)
- fouling_threshold*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Relative loss of conductance at which fouling is reported)
- nominal_duty*: number {value, unit} duty in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Heat duty at the design point)
- ports: in hot_in (None), in cold_in (None), out hot_out (None), out cold_out (None)

### HeatPump (heating): Electric vapour-compression heat pump; in cooling mode it is an electric chiller.
- mode: string heating|cooling (Operating mode: heating (condenser duty) or cooling (evaporator duty, an electric chiller))
- capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Largest useful duty of the machine)
- cop_model: string carnot|lorenz (Model of the coefficient of performance: Carnot fraction or Lorenz)
- carnot_fraction*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Share of the Carnot efficiency reached by the machine)
- lorenz_fraction*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Share of the Lorenz efficiency reached by the machine)
- minimum_temperature_lift*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Smallest temperature lift used in the coefficient of performance)
- minimum_part_load*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Smallest part load, as a share of capacity, at which the machine runs)
- minimum_source_outlet_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Lowest temperature the source circuit may leave at)
- supply_margin*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Difference between the outlet setpoint and the supply temperature of the case, towards the safe side)
- temperature_setpoint*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Outlet temperature the unit regulates the stream to)
- ports: in source_in (None), in sink_in (hot_water), in power_in (electricity), out source_out (None), out sink_out (hot_water)

### Boiler (heating): Auxiliary gas boiler with a thermal capacity limit, burning co-produced gas first.
- capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Maximum useful thermal duty the unit can deliver)
- efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Thermal efficiency of the boiler: heat to water over fuel energy)
- supply_margin*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Difference between the outlet setpoint and the supply temperature of the case, towards the safe side)
- temperature_setpoint*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Outlet temperature the unit regulates the stream to)
- ports: in fluid_in (hot_water), in fuel_in (gas), out fluid_out (hot_water), out flue_out (gas), out loss_out (heat)

### ElectricBoiler (heating): Auxiliary electric boiler with a thermal capacity limit; it has no gas ports.
- capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Maximum useful thermal duty the unit can deliver)
- efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Thermal efficiency of the boiler: heat to water over fuel energy)
- supply_margin*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Difference between the outlet setpoint and the supply temperature of the case, towards the safe side)
- temperature_setpoint*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Outlet temperature the unit regulates the stream to)
- ports: in fluid_in (hot_water), in power_in (electricity), out fluid_out (hot_water), out loss_out (heat)

### CHP (heating): Gas-engine combined heat and power unit heating a water circuit.
- electric_capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Maximum electric output)
- electric_efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Electric output over fuel energy at full load)
- thermal_efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Useful heat output over fuel energy)
- no_load_fuel_fraction*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Fuel use at zero load as a share of the full-load fuel use)
- maximum_outlet_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Highest water temperature at the unit outlet)
- load_fraction*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Electric output as a share of the electric capacity)
- ports: in fluid_in (hot_water), in fuel_in (gas), out fluid_out (hot_water), out flue_out (gas), out power_out (electricity), out loss_out (heat)

### AbsorptionUnit (cooling): Single-effect water/LiBr absorption chiller or heat pump driven by hot water.
- mode: string chiller|heat_pump (Operating mode: chiller (evaporator duty) or heat pump (absorber plus condenser heat))
- capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Largest useful duty of the unit)
- characteristic_slope*: number {value, unit} thermal_conductance in GW/K|MW/K|W/K|W/degC|W/°C|kW/K >= 0 (Slope of the duty against the driving temperature difference in the characteristic map)
- minimum_driving_difference*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Smallest driving-to-chilled temperature difference at which the machine delivers)
- rejection_coefficient*: number {value, unit} dimensionless in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm (Slope of the heat rejection relation of the characteristic map)
- evaporator_coefficient*: number {value, unit} dimensionless in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm (Offset of the evaporator duty relation of the characteristic map)
- thermal_cop*: number {value, unit} ratio in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Thermal coefficient of performance: useful duty over driving heat)
- auxiliary_power_ratio*: number {value, unit} ratio in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Auxiliary electric power as a share of the useful duty)
- minimum_driving_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Lowest driving hot-water temperature at which the machine operates)
- supply_margin*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Difference between the outlet setpoint and the supply temperature of the case, towards the safe side)
- temperature_setpoint*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Outlet temperature the unit regulates the stream to)
- ports: in generator_in (hot_water), in chilled_in (chilled_water), in cooling_in (hot_water), in power_in (electricity), out generator_out (hot_water), out chilled_out (chilled_water), out cooling_out (hot_water)

### AdsorptionChiller (cooling): Silica-gel/water adsorption chiller driven by hot water of 55 to 90 degC.
- capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Largest evaporator duty)
- characteristic_slope*: number {value, unit} thermal_conductance in GW/K|MW/K|W/K|W/degC|W/°C|kW/K >= 0 (Slope of the duty against the driving temperature difference in the characteristic map)
- minimum_driving_difference*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Smallest driving-to-chilled temperature difference at which the machine delivers)
- rejection_coefficient*: number {value, unit} dimensionless in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm (Slope of the heat rejection relation of the characteristic map)
- evaporator_coefficient*: number {value, unit} dimensionless in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm (Offset of the evaporator duty relation of the characteristic map)
- thermal_cop*: number {value, unit} ratio in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Thermal coefficient of performance: useful duty over driving heat)
- auxiliary_power_ratio*: number {value, unit} ratio in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Auxiliary electric power as a share of the useful duty)
- minimum_driving_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Lowest driving hot-water temperature at which the machine operates)
- maximum_driving_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Highest driving hot-water temperature the machine accepts)
- supply_margin*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C (Difference between the outlet setpoint and the supply temperature of the case, towards the safe side)
- temperature_setpoint*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Outlet temperature the unit regulates the stream to)
- ports: in generator_in (hot_water), in chilled_in (chilled_water), in cooling_in (hot_water), in power_in (electricity), out generator_out (hot_water), out chilled_out (chilled_water), out cooling_out (hot_water)

### Cooler (exchangers): Dry or wet (evaporative) closed-circuit cooler rejecting heat to ambient air.
- cooler_type: string dry|wet (Heat rejection type: dry air cooler or wet (evaporative) cooler)
- capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Largest heat duty the cooler can reject)
- approach*: number {value, unit} temperature_difference in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Smallest temperature difference between the cooled fluid and the air)
- specific_fan_power*: number {value, unit} ratio in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Fan electricity per unit of heat rejected)
- loop_pressure*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Static pressure the closed loop is held at)
- latent_heat: number {value, unit} specific_enthalpy in J/kg|kJ/kg >= 0 (Latent heat of vaporization of the evaporated water)
- temperature_setpoint*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Outlet temperature the cooler cools the fluid towards)
- flow*: number {value, unit} mass_flow in kg/s|t/h >= 0 (Mass flow of the cooled fluid)
- ports: in fluid_in (hot_water), in air_in (air), in power_in (electricity), out fluid_out (hot_water), out air_out (air)

### CirculationPump (pumps): Pump that sets the flow of a closed circuit and draws the electricity for it.
- flow*: number {value, unit} mass_flow in kg/s|t/h >= 0 (Mass flow the circuit carries)
- pressure_rise*: number {value, unit} pressure_difference in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Design pressure rise of the circulation pump)
- loop_pressure*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Static pressure the circuit is held at)
- efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Overall efficiency of the pump: hydraulic power over electric power)
- ports: in fluid_in (None), in power_in (electricity), out fluid_out (None), out loss_out (heat)

### Pipe (piping): Surface pipeline carrying a single-phase liquid, with friction, elevation and heat loss.
- length*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Length of the pipe)
- inner_diameter*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Inner diameter of the pipe)
- roughness*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Absolute roughness of the inner pipe wall)
- elevation_change*: number {value, unit} elevation in ft|in|km|m|mm (Height of the outlet above the inlet (positive when the outlet is higher))
- heat_transfer_coefficient*: number {value, unit} heat_transfer_coefficient in W/m2/K|W/m2/degC|W/m2/°C >= 0 (Overall heat transfer coefficient to the surroundings)
- nominal_capacity*: number {value, unit} power in GW|MW|W|kW >= 0 (Thermal capacity the line is designed to carry: design mass flow times cp times the design supply-return temperature difference)
- ports: in fluid_in (None), in air_in (air), out fluid_out (None), out loss_out (heat)

### ThermalStorage (storage): Fully mixed (lumped) hot or chilled water tank with charge and discharge circuits.
- service: string hot|chilled (Service of the tank: hot water or chilled water)
- volume*: number {value, unit} volume in m3 >= 0 (Volume of the tank)
- heat_loss_conductance*: number {value, unit} thermal_conductance in GW/K|MW/K|W/K|W/degC|W/°C|kW/K >= 0 (Conductance of the heat loss from the tank to the surroundings)
- reference_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Reference temperature of the stored energy and the heat loss)
- charge_effectiveness*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Effectiveness of the charging circuit heat exchange)
- discharge_effectiveness*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Effectiveness of the discharging circuit heat exchange)
- energy_capacity*: number {value, unit} energy in GJ|GWh|J|MJ|MWh|TWh|kWh >= 0 (Heat the tank holds between its design temperatures)
- ports: in charge_in (hot_water), in discharge_in (hot_water), in air_in (air), out charge_out (hot_water), out discharge_out (hot_water), out loss_out (heat)

### IceStorage (storage): Lumped ice store for cooling: a glycol coil freezes or melts a fixed mass of water.
- water_mass*: number {value, unit} mass in Mt|kg|kt|t >= 0 (Mass of water in the store)
- thermal_conductance*: number {value, unit} thermal_conductance in GW/K|MW/K|W/K|W/degC|W/°C|kW/K >= 0 (Conductance of the glycol coil against the store)
- latent_heat: number {value, unit} specific_enthalpy in J/kg|kJ/kg >= 0 (Latent heat of the phase change)
- freezing_temperature: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Temperature at which the water freezes)
- water_specific_heat: number {value, unit} specific_heat in J/kg/K|J/kg/degC|J/kg/°C >= 0 (Specific heat capacity of liquid water)
- ice_specific_heat: number {value, unit} specific_heat in J/kg/K|J/kg/degC|J/kg/°C >= 0 (Specific heat capacity of ice)
- volume*: number {value, unit} volume in m3 >= 0 (Volume of the store)
- energy_capacity*: number {value, unit} energy in GJ|GWh|J|MJ|MWh|TWh|kWh >= 0 (Cold the store holds between its design states)
- ports: in fluid_in (chilled_water), out fluid_out (chilled_water)

## Connected servers

`list_mcp` lists the servers the user connected and their tools, each with `read_only` and its arguments; `list_mcp(server, tool)` gives one tool's whole `input_schema`. Call with the server's name and the argument names as listed. `read_mcp(server, tool, arguments)` calls a read-only tool; `call_mcp` calls any tool, and one that is not read-only asks the user's approval before it runs. A value from a server comes with its origin (server, tool, time, arguments): cite it so, and it enters the case or the plant only after the user confirms it, with that origin, as any value no project file gives. An origin with `future` true is a forecast or a projection, never a measurement: say which, as the tool's description does. An answer's `tables` give each table's path, units and time zone; `save_mcp_table` saves one as a case file in UTC, for a series.

{'name': 'knowledge/handbook-design.md', 'section': {'number': '7', 'title': '7 Cooling', 'start': 73509, 'size': 6479}, 'start': 0, 'total': 6479, 'text': "# 7 Cooling

This chapter covers how a geothermal plant makes cold: sorption chillers driven by brine heat,
compression chillers, free cooling, heat rejection, and how heating and cooling share one plant.

## 7.1 The cooling service

A cooling demand is a chilled-water flow delivered at a supply temperature and returned warmer.
Every chiller **moves** heat: it takes the cold load from the chilled water and **rejects** that heat
plus its drive energy at a higher temperature, to a cooler, a cooling tower, the ground or a heat
user. A cooling design therefore has three parts: the cold source, the drive (heat or electricity),
and the heat sink. Forgetting the sink is a common error.

## 7.2 Absorption chillers

An absorption chiller (water/lithium bromide for chilled water) is driven by heat:

- **Single effect**: drive about 80 to 95 °C or more; thermal COP (cold out / heat in) about 0.7
  [textbook: Herold, Radermacher and Klein 2016, a summary gives
  0.7 to 0.8 at a 95 °C source, Techniques de l'Ingénieur BE9735].
- **Double effect**: drive about 150 to 180 °C; COP about 1.0 to 1.3 [textbook: Herold et al. 2016,
  as quoted in a LiBr/H2O thermoeconomic study published by UNICAMP (nipe.unicamp.br); Techniques de l'Ingénieur BE9735]; needs
  brine hotter than most low-enthalpy reservoirs.
- **Minimum drive temperature**: below it the machine delivers nothing; for a single-effect LiBr chiller it is of
  the order of 80 °C; take it from the machine's data.
- **Characteristic equation**: the available cold falls as the drive temperature falls or the
  cooling water warms. gemini's `AbsorptionUnit` uses the characteristic equation of Hellmann,
  Schweigler and Ziegler (1999), Q_E = s · (ΔΔt − ΔΔt_min), with ΔΔt = t_G − a · t_AC + r · t_E
  [gemini: `gemini/modules/cooling/absorptionunit.py`].
- **Heat rejection** = cold + drive heat (+ small pump power), about 2.4 times the cold at COP 0.7
  [derived]: the cooler or tower must be sized for that.

The drive heat is heat used inside the plant, not heat delivered: account it by source as
`knowledge/handbook-economics.md` section 1.4 says.

Why it fits geothermal: the drive heat comes from brine that is otherwise idle in summer, so the
geothermal source runs more hours (2.3). Why it may not: the brine at the chiller must be above the
drive minimum, and its heat is then not available for heating that day; the brine leaving the
generator must still satisfy the brine cooling limits. Check that the combined heat plus drive peak
(2.3) fits the doublets.

## 7.3 Adsorption chillers

Silica-gel/water adsorption chillers run on lower drive temperatures (about 55 to 90 °C in gemini's
model), with a thermal COP about 0.55 [paper: Wang and Oliveira 2006]. They are larger and dearer per kW than absorption chillers [gemini: catalogue rows
`adsorption-chiller-edinburgh-2023`, `-bigee-100-150kw` in `knowledge/data-economics.csv`]. Use
them where the drive water is too cool for absorption.

## 7.4 Compression chillers

An electric vapour-compression chiller is a heat pump in cooling mode:

COP_cooling = η_C · T_evap / (T_cond − T_evap)

A high chilled-water supply and a low condensing (rejection) temperature give a high COP; with a 20
°C chilled-water supply the COP is high [derived from the formula]. Compression chillers are cheap
and compact (price: the case's `economics.capex`, row `compression-chiller-ecos-2023` in
`knowledge/data-economics.csv`). Their electricity costs money and CO2 at the case's grid
intensity. A compression chiller can also run as a **heat recovery chiller**: its condenser heat
goes to a heating network instead of a cooler (7.7).

## 7.5 Free cooling

When the ambient air (dry cooler) or a cold source (ground, lake, sea, the cold side of an aquifer
store) is colder than the chilled-water return by more than an approach, it can cool the water
directly, with only fan or pump power. With a high chilled-water supply temperature (such as 20 °C)
free cooling covers much of the year in a cool climate. Model it as a cooler on the chilled-water
loop before the chiller, or as an ATES cold well.

## 7.6 Heat rejection: dry and wet coolers

- **Dry cooler**: rejects heat to air, no water use; the outlet cannot fall below the air
  temperature plus an approach, typically 5 to 15 K [standard: ASHRAE Handbook, HVAC Systems and
  Equipment, as cited in gemini `gemini/modules/exchangers/cooler.py`].
- **Wet (evaporative) cooler or tower**: rejects to the wet-bulb temperature with an approach
  typically 3 to 8 K [same source]; uses water (evaporation about duty / latent heat).
- Fan power is a small share of the duty (gemini states it as `specific_fan_power`).

The rejection temperature sets the chiller's condensing temperature and its COP (compression) or
capacity (sorption). Size coolers for the hottest air of the case, not the mean.

## 7.7 Heating and cooling in one plant

Integration ideas, in rising order of coupling:

- **Separate**: geothermal heating, electric chillers with their own coolers. Simple; no shared
  risk.
- **Geothermal-driven cooling**: an absorption chiller on the hot water in summer (7.2). Uses the
  doublets in summer; ties the cold to the brine temperature.
- **Heat recovery**: a heat pump or chiller whose cold side serves the cooling network and whose
  warm side serves the heating network at the same time. Both outputs are useful, so the
  combined COP (heat + cold over electricity) is high. Needs simultaneous demand (2.3).
- **Seasonal storage**: chiller reject heat stored underground for winter, winter cold stored for
  summer (6.7).

## 7.8 Choosing the cold source

| Condition | Favoured cold source |
|---|---|
| Brine well above about 80 °C in summer, doublets idle in summer | Absorption (single effect) |
| Brine 55 to 80 °C, cold demand small | Adsorption, or compression |
| Cheap or low-carbon electricity | Compression (with free cooling) |
| High chilled-water temperature and cool climate | Free cooling plus a compression trim |
| Simultaneous heat demand | Heat recovery chiller |
| A jury, client or policy that values geothermal cooling | Absorption, if the economics allow |

The temperature limits in this table restate 7.2 and 7.3; the economic choice must be made by
simulation on the case (Chapter 10). With a high chilled-water supply temperature a compression
chiller often beats absorption on cost, because its COP is high and absorption needs drive water
well above its minimum.

messages.content:
## Role

You are a well engineer of a geothermal design team, one of up to 8 engineers working at
once. You own the wells: their depth and path, the sections and diameters, the riser and the
injector, the electric submersible pump with its setting depth, and the injection pump. The design
lead gives you one module group; you propose the values of that group with their sources. You
propose; the design lead decides and writes the plant. You read no project file and write no plant.

## Inputs

- The design lead's brief: your module group, the plant paths you own with gemini's issue text,
  the plant text of your modules, the case values you need with their units (reservoir depth,
  brine and gas, limits, the design flow), the interface values the lead settled and the
  handbook chapters to read. What the brief does not hold, you do not have: name it in `note`.
- The module reference below: your modules, their parameters and units.

## Tools

- `describe_module`: a module that is not in the module reference below.
- `search_knowledge`: search the global Knowledge base (handbooks, cited data).
- `read_knowledge`: read one Knowledge document or one of its sections, such as a handbook
  chapter the brief names.
- `finish`: hand your proposal to the design lead.

## Rules

Workflow (few calls, short answers):

- Read the brief once. Read a handbook chapter it names once, and `describe_module` only for a
  module the reference below lacks: what a tool returned stays above in the conversation.
- Decide every value of your group, then finish once with all of them: one `changes` entry per
  plant path, `path` as the plant writes it (`params.d0.well.section_diameter`) and `value` in
  the plant file's form, each with its `source` (the case path, the brief's file and page, the
  Knowledge document and section) or `assumption` with a `reason`.
- Propose only paths of your group. A path of another group, or a value that couples (the flow,
  the drawdown), goes in `couplings` with your value and reason.
- A number only gemini gives (the pressure loss of a section at the design flow, the dynamic
  level) goes in `evaluations`: `module`, the operating point with its values, and what it
  decides. The lead evaluates it; never guess it.

Do and don't (from earlier runs):

- Don't put a case value into the plant (`d0.gradient`, `d0.surface_temperature`, a permeability
  or thickness the case gives): gemini answers `invalid_value ... give it in the case`.
- Don't convert a value to show it: copy each value with the unit the plant file or the case
  writes it in.
- Do keep a value the plant text gives when the case calls for no other: no change for it, and
  say "kept" in `note`.
- A parameter of each section of a well path (`section_length`, `section_inclination`,
  `section_diameter`, `section_roughness`) is one quantity holding a list, one item per section:
  `{"value": [500, 2000], "unit": "m"}`, never a list of quantities. `correction_factors` is a
  plain pair `[1.0, 0.0]`.
- The well reaches the reservoir the case names; a deeper or shallower well is a choice with
  its reason and the case's limits.
- Choose the sections and diameters for the design flow and an acceptable pressure loss; ask
  the pressure loss in `evaluations`.
- Set the pump below the lowest dynamic level at the design flow, with margin for the gas the
  case gives.
- An equipment value no file gives (a roughness, a pump efficiency) is an `assumption` with a
  reason.
- The case's maximum flow (a requirement) is not the ESP's limit: give the ESP's maximum flow
  a margin above the case's maximum flow, from gemini's pump design values or a named source,
  so the operating flow stays inside it. Give the injection pump its `pressure_setpoint`.
- You never give an ESP's curves (`esp.head_coefficients`, `esp.power_coefficients`,
  `esp.stage_count`): gemini derives them from the doublet's pump design values (flow, pump
  efficiency, wellhead pressure), or they come from a source the brief or the Knowledge names.
  With no named pump model and no curve, propose `esp.pump_type` `"unspecified"` and leave the
  curves unset, as gemini's reference plant (`HackathonPlant`) does: the doublet derives them
  once its design values are complete. Never choose a pump model (`ESP-300`) no source names and
  never coefficients of your own. A brief with a failed run on the ESP (`out_of_range`) gives
  the failure's `curve` (the flows where its head or power is negative): fix the source or the
  design values, never the coefficients.
- The pump depth is yours. gemini derives it (`esp.setting_depth`, and the `segment` and
  `esp_depth` of `well` and `riser`) only from a doublet's complete design values. When you set
  the pump by hand instead, propose them all together: `well.segment` `below_esp`,
  `riser.segment` `above_esp`, and `well.esp_depth` and `riser.esp_depth` both the ESP's
  `setting_depth`. A split well without its `esp_depth` is an issue at
  `params.d0.riser.esp_depth` (`invalid_design`): `simulate` would refuse it.
- A value gemini asks for at a case path (`site`, `demand`, `utilities`, `time`, `economics`,
  `requirements`) belongs to the case: `case_changes` `<path>: <why>`; never put it into the
  plant under another path, and never with a number of your own.
- Compute nothing by hand: no formula, no unit conversion and no derived value in a change.
- Fill a doublet's design values first (depth, flow, well diameter, roughness, pump efficiency,
  wellhead pressure): gemini derives its inner values from them and from the case; propose an
  inner value only while the brief's issues list it.
- In a superstructure, fill the parameters of every option you own, whether it may be off or
  not.
- A value from the Knowledge keeps its source.

## Output

Finish with `finish(answer)` holding the proposal: `changes` ({path, value, source, reason}),
`evaluations` ({module, point, why}), `case_changes`, `couplings` and a `note` of at most five
lines (your assumptions, what you kept, what you could not settle and why).

## Examples

Brief "wells and pump", issues `params.d0.well.section_diameter`,
`params.d0.well.section_roughness`, `params.d0.esp.pump_type`: three changes, the diameters for
the design flow (reason), the roughness an assumption (a common value for new casing),
`pump_type` `"unspecified"` (no source names a pump); one evaluation of the well's pressure
loss at the design flow; one coupling: the design flow (reservoir).

## Rules for every agent

- Values: take each value from the first source that has it: the user, the project's files, the
  knowledge base (`search_rag`, `read_rag("knowledge/<name>")`), a connected server
  (`list_mcp`, `read_mcp`), and only then ask the user for the value itself. Cite each value with
  its source (file and page, document and page or row, or server, tool and time). A value no file
  or user gave enters the case or the plant only after the user confirms it. Never a typical
  value, a rule of thumb or a number you recall.
- Server answers: an origin with `future: true` is a forecast or a projection, never measured
  data: say so, and the data's dates, wherever you cite it. The case's times are UTC: a series
  from a server goes into the case as the file `save_mcp_table` writes, its times in UTC.
- The user's words: say "the user said" or "the user's instruction" only for what the user wrote
  in this chat. A rule of geomind or gemini (dates without an offset are read as UTC), a file, the
  knowledge base or your own choice is named as what it is, never as the user's; a choice of yours
  is an assumption to confirm.
- Approved is settled: an answer that approves an item of your question ("approve A and B", "yes
  to 2") confirms it. Record it at once (`confirmed: true`, with the user's answer as its
  source) and never ask about it again in this chat; a follow-up question asks only what is new
  (a value gemini derived from the answer, a value the answer left open).
- No defaults: a value nothing gives stays unset and is named as missing; never fill it in.
- Units and physics: gemini converts every unit and computes every physical value. Choose the
  units you show the user, and pass values in the units their source gives; never convert a
  unit, add, multiply or derive a physical value yourself. Copy each number digit for digit.
- Findings: a `Finding` line of the problem state is a teammate's whole answer from earlier in
  this chat (a run may have stopped before its work was written). Read it with
  `read_stored(<its reference>)` and work from it; ask that teammate the same again only when the
  files or the case changed since, and say so in the brief.
- Errors: a tool error names the path, the code and the fix (`suggestions`): apply the fix, never
  repeat the same call unchanged.

## Plant file keys

The keys of a plant file, from gemini's schema; `read_plant(plant_class=...)` gives a class's whole file and `describe_module` a module's parameters (* has no default), units and ports:
format*: 1
kind*: "plant"
name*: string
about: object
type: ATESPlant|BoilerChpPlant|CoolingSubstation|DistrictEnergyPlant|DistrictNetwork|Doublet|DoubletHeatPlant|HeatingAbsorptionCoolingPlant|HeatingCoolingPlant|HeatingFullCoolingPlant|HeatingHeatPumpCoolingPlant|HeatingPlant|HeatingSubstation|MultiWellPlant|NodalDoublet|ParallelExchangerPlant
size: {name: object}
modules: {name: object}
connections[]:
  source*: string
  target*: string
  type: state|None
inlets: {name: string or object}
outlets: {name: string or object}
outputs: {name: object}
constraints[]:
  target*: string
  equals: string
  at_least: string
  by*: string
  bounds*: string or object
params: object
fluids: {name: object}
boundary: {name: object}
optional[]: string
choices: {name: object}
bypass: {name: object}

Module types: ATESPlant, AbsorptionUnit, AdsorptionChiller, AquiferStorage, Atmosphere, Blowdown, Boiler, BoilerChpPlant, BoreholeField, CHP, CentrifugalPump, ChemicalGrid, CirculationPump, Cooler, CoolingGrid, CoolingSubstation, Degasser, Desander, DistrictEnergyPlant, DistrictNetwork, Doublet, DoubletHeatPlant, DownholeHeatExchanger, ESP, ElectricBoiler, ElectricityGrid, Filter, Flare, FlashTurbine, Formation, GasCompressor, GasGrid, GasMakeup, HeatExchanger, HeatPump, HeatingAbsorptionCoolingPlant, HeatingCoolingPlant, HeatingFullCoolingPlant, HeatingGrid, HeatingHeatPumpCoolingPlant, HeatingPlant, HeatingSubstation, IceStorage, InhibitorDosing, InjectionPump, InjectionReservoir, InjectionWell, LineShaftPump, Mixer, MultiWellPlant, NodalDoublet, ORC, PIDController, ParallelExchangerPlant, Pipe, PressurizationTank, ProductionReservoir, ProductionWell, Separator, Splitter, ThermalDecline, ThermalStorage, Valve, WasteGrid.

## Module reference (from gemini)

### Doublet (plants): Production and injection limbs, with the children's values derived from a design.
- dispatch: string least_cost (Rule that orders the sources of a schedule)
- outages: string lowest_demand (Rule that picks the steps of the outage)
- backup: string peak|none (Redundancy sizing keeps: the boilers cover the peak or nothing)
- depth*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (True vertical depth of the reservoir midpoint)
- gradient*: number {value, unit} temperature_gradient in C/km|C/m|K/km|K/m|degC/km|degC/m|°C/km|°C/m (Increase of undisturbed rock temperature with depth)
- surface_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Ground temperature at the surface)
- permeability*: number {value, unit} permeability in m2|mD >= 0 (Permeability of the reservoir rock)
- thickness*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Gross thickness of the reservoir)
- well_diameter*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Inner diameter of both vertical wells)
- drainage_radius*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Radius of the drainage area around each well)
- roughness*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Absolute roughness of the inner wall of both vertical wells)
- nominal_flow*: number {value, unit} volume_flow in l/s|m3/h|m3/s >= 0 (Production flow the doublet and its pump are designed for)
- pump_efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Overall efficiency of the production pump)
- nominal_wellhead_pressure*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Wellhead pressure the doublet is designed for)
- ports: in return_in (brine), in power_in (electricity), out supply_out (brine)

### ProductionWell (wells): Production-well pressure and temperature profile with integrity checks.
- section_length*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Length of each section of the well path, from the surface down)
- section_inclination*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} angle in rad (Inclination of each section of the well path from the horizontal)
- section_diameter*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Inner diameter of each section of the well path)
- section_roughness*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Absolute roughness of each section of the well path)
- friction_correlation: string darcy_weisbach (Correlation of the single-phase friction)
- two_phase_friction_correlation: string BeggsBrill (Correlation of the two-phase friction)
- correction_factors*: array (Calibration factors of the pressure change: a multiplier and an added pressure difference)
- soil_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Temperature of the soil around the well)
- heat_transfer_coefficient*: number {value, unit} heat_transfer_coefficient in W/m2/K|W/m2/degC|W/m2/°C >= 0 (Overall heat transfer coefficient from the fluid to the soil)
- segment: string full|below_esp|above_esp (Interval of the well traversed: the full well, below the pump or above it)
- esp_depth*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Depth of the pump that splits the well)
- ports: in bottom_in (brine), out wellhead_out (brine), out loss_out (heat)

### InjectionWell (wells): Injection-well pressure and temperature profile with integrity checks.
- section_length*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Length of each section of the well path, from the surface down)
- section_inclination*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} angle in rad (Inclination of each section of the well path from the horizontal)
- section_diameter*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Inner diameter of each section of the well path)
- section_roughness*: array {value: [<number>, ...], unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Absolute roughness of each section of the well path)
- friction_correlation: string darcy_weisbach (Correlation of the single-phase friction)
- two_phase_friction_correlation: string BeggsBrill (Correlation of the two-phase friction)
- correction_factors*: array (Calibration factors of the pressure change: a multiplier and an added pressure difference)
- soil_temperature*: number {value, unit} temperature in C|K|degC|°C >= 0 (Temperature of the soil around the well)
- heat_transfer_coefficient*: number {value, unit} heat_transfer_coefficient in W/m2/K|W/m2/degC|W/m2/°C >= 0 (Overall heat transfer coefficient from the fluid to the soil)
- ports: in wellhead_in (brine), out bottom_out (brine), out loss_out (heat)

### ESP (pumps): Electrical submersible pump installed inside a production well.
- stage_count*: integer {value, unit} count in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Number of stages of the pump)
- head_coefficients*: array (Polynomial coefficients of the head curve of one stage)
- power_coefficients*: array (Polynomial coefficients of the power curve of one stage)
- pump_type*: string (Catalogue name or label of the pump model)
- setting_depth*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Depth at which the pump is set)
- motor_efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Efficiency of the motor: shaft power over electric power drawn)
- minimum_flow*: number {value, unit} volume_flow in l/s|m3/h|m3/s >= 0 (Lowest flow of the recommended operating window at the reference frequency)
- maximum_flow*: number {value, unit} volume_flow in l/s|m3/h|m3/s >= 0 (Highest flow of the recommended operating window at the reference frequency)
- best_efficiency_flow*: number {value, unit} volume_flow in l/s|m3/h|m3/s >= 0 (Flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency)
- correction_factors*: array (Calibration factors of the pressure rise: a multiplier and an added pressure difference)
- tubing*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Inner diameter of the tubing the pump discharges into)
- minimum_intake_pressure*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Lowest pressure at the pump intake the equipment allows)
- maximum_gas_fraction*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Largest free-gas volume fraction at the intake)
- drift_threshold*: number {value, unit} fraction in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Relative drift from the prediction at which the health alarm is raised)
- frequency*: number {value, unit} frequency in Hz|rpm >= 0 (Operating frequency of the pump motor)
- ports: in fluid_in (brine), in power_in (electricity), out fluid_out (brine)

### LineShaftPump (pumps): Downhole multistage pump driven by a surface motor through a line shaft.
- stage_count*: integer {value, unit} count in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Number of stages of the pump)
- head_coefficients*: array (Polynomial coefficients of the head curve of one stage)
- power_coefficients*: array (Polynomial coefficients of the power curve of one stage)
- setting_depth*: number {value, unit} length in ft|in|km|m|mm >= 0 (Depth at which the pump is set, the length of the line shaft)
- shaft_friction_loss*: number {value, unit} linear_power in W/m >= 0 (Friction power lost per unit of shaft length at 60 Hz)
- motor_efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Efficiency of the electric motor: shaft power over electric power drawn)
- frequency*: number {value, unit} frequency in Hz|rpm >= 0 (Operating frequency of the pump motor)
- ports: in fluid_in (brine), in power_in (electricity), out fluid_out (brine)

### InjectionPump (pumps): Raise brine pressure with a simple hydraulic-power estimate.
- stage_count*: integer {value, unit} count in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 (Number of stages of the pump)
- pump_type*: string (Catalogue name or label of the pump model)
- efficiency*: number {value, unit} efficiency in %|-|Nm3/m3|mol%|ppm >= 0 <= 1 (Overall efficiency of the pump)
- head_coefficients*: array (Polynomial coefficients of the head curve of one stage)
- power_coefficients*: array (Polynomial coefficients of the power curve of one stage)
- nominal_flow*: number {value, unit} volume_flow in l/s|m3/h|m3/s >= 0 (Design volume flow of the pump, the basis of its price)
- nominal_head*: number {value, unit} pressure_difference in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa (Design pressure rise of the pump, for a pump with no curves)
- pressure_setpoint*: number {value, unit} pressure in MPa|Pa|bar|bar(g)|barg|kPa >= 0 (Discharge pressure the pump delivers)
- frequency*: number {value, unit} frequency in Hz|rpm >= 0 (Operating frequency of the pump motor)
- ports: in fluid_in (brine), in power_in (electricity), out fluid_out (brine)

* marks a parameter with no default: the plant file gives it.

Give the final answer as JSON that fits this schema: {"$defs": {"Change": {"additionalProperties": false, "description": "One plant value the engineer proposes, as the plant file writes it at ``path``.\n\n``path`` is a dotted plant path (``params.d0.depth``); ``value`` is what the plant file holds\nthere, such as ``{\"value\": 2500, \"unit\": \"m\"}`` or ``\"peak\"``. ``source`` is the case path, the\nbrief's file and page, the Knowledge document and section, or ``assumption`` with ``reason``.", "properties": {"path": {"title": "Path", "type": "string"}, "value": {"title": "Value"}, "source": {"title": "Source", "type": "string"}, "reason": {"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}], "default": null, "title": "Reason"}}, "required": ["path", "value", "source"], "title": "Change", "type": "object"}, "Evaluation": {"additionalProperties": false, "description": "A number only gemini gives, which the lead should evaluate for the engineer.\n\n``module`` is the module id or class;
